Smart Look At The Week Ahead: Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Coca-Cola And Starbucks
article:
There will be a big decision facing Kevin Warsh and the Fed Open Market Committee. Will he and the rate-setting committee have enough courage to hike the Fed fund rate ahead of the mid-term elections? It will be a tough call to strike the right balance between delicate political pressures and pressing economic issues.
Whilst the Fed could chicken out on hiking rates, the Bank of Canada is expected to lift the overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%. The Canadian central bank is concerned about the economy, but it could also be more worried about inflation. In September, the rate of inflation rose to 3.1%.
The European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan will also have interest-rate decisions to make. At its last meeting, the ECB said it is keeping all its options open. Meanwhile, the BoJ faced some pushback when it hiked its short-term rate at the last meeting. It could keep rates unchanged at the October meeting, if only to keep the peace.
The UK will announce its latest budget. The government has not ruled out tax rises. It has not ruled out expenditure cuts, either. So, it could be a budget for austerity as the UK faces higher borrowing costs.
On the corporate front
It is a busy earnings week with some top names from the tech, pharmaceutical, financial and consumer staples sectors on the chopping board.
Alphabet
(Nasdaq: GOOG) is set to report third-quarter numbers. The main focus of attention will be growth at its cloud business. The market will also be scrutinising the company’s AI capital expenditure. Investors will want to see some evidence of a decent return on investment.
Microsoft
(Nasdaq: MSFT) will also be under the microscope when it reports first-quarter numbers. It is expected to report double-digit increases in both revenue and earnings per share. But close attention will be paid to the software giant’s Azure cloud computing business, its Copilot services and the amount of money it is spending to support demand for its AI data centres.
Staying with the Mag 7,
Amazon
(Nasdaq: AMZN) will report third-quarter numbers. Strong earnings growth is expected from the online retailer. But all eyes could be on Amazon Web Service. Importantly, capital expenditure could be the primary concern, after the company reported that free cash flow has turned negative.
Other tech companies to watch include chipmaker
Intel
(Nasdaq: INTC), which will report third-quarter numbers and data-storage company
Seagate
(Nasdaq: STX) with first-quarter earnings. Telecom outfit
Verizon
(NYSE: VZ) will report third-quarter results and
American Tower
(NYSEM AMT) will step in with third-quarter earnings, too.
Coca-Cola
(NYSE: KO) will bring home its third-quarter report card. The fizzy-drinks maker has the wind in its sails, with earnings and revenue expected to improve again. The market will be looking for volume growth and expansion in operating margin. Elsewhere, the market will be looking for more signs that the nascent turnaround is progressing at
Starbucks
(Nasdaq: SBUX) when it reports fourth-quarter numbers.
There should be no surprises when a trio of oil companies turn on the taps with third-quarter earnings.
Shell
(NYSE: SHEL),
ExxonMobil
(NYSE: XOM) and
BP
(NYSE: BP) will get the ball rolling. High oil prices should provide the necessary fuel for earnings growth, as margins soar at the three integrated oil companies.
Visa
(NYSE: V) and
MasterCard
(NYSE: MA) could provide valuable insights into the spending habits of households when they report full-year and third-quarter results. Meanwhile,
HSBC
(SEHK: 0005) and
Standard Chartered
(SEHK: 2888) are expected to highlight growth at its wealth-management businesses as the rich get increasingly richer.
Other companies to watch include
GSK
(NYSE: GSK),
Eli Lilly
(NYSE: LLY)
, Merck
(NYSE: MRK) and
Bristol Meyer Squibb
(NYSE: BMY) from the pharmaceutical sector, and
Ford
(NYSE: F)and
Stellantis
(NYSE: STLA) from the car-making arena.
At the local level, a bunch of REITs are set to announce results. They include
CapitaLand Ascott Trust
(SGX: HMN),
Mapletree Industrial Trust
(SGX: ME8U) and
Mapletree Pan Asia Commercial Trust
(SGX: N2IU).

title: Top Stock Market Highlights of the Week: Haze Probe on Plantation Stocks, EQDP, Keppel REIT, iFAST and Getty Images
article:
Haze returned to Singapore, and with it came a sharp warning to listed plantation companies that their financing and investor standing may be targeted.
Elsewhere, the
Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP)
reported early progress in drawing private capital, Keppel REIT unveiled a major office purchase from its sponsor, and iFAST stepped into ETF issuance.
In the US, Getty Images began a pre-packaged bankruptcy to restructure its debt and go private.
Government turns up the pressure on plantation stocks linked to haze
The Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) has sought information from seven listed agriculture companies about possible links to the Indonesian forest fires behind Singapore’s haze.
Senior Minister K Shanmugam spoke about the move on 19 October 2026.
The seven are
Golden Agri-Resources
(SGX: E5H),
Bumitama Agri
(SGX: P8Z),
First Resources
(SGX: EB5),
Wilmar International
(SGX: F34),
Kencana Agri
(SGX: BNE),
Indofood Agri Resources
(SGX: 5JS) and
TSH Resources
(SGX: TSH).
The government will also scrutinise Singapore-incorporated Asia Pulp & Paper. Three of its pulpwood suppliers were among the Indonesian firms named the previous week.
Mr Shanmugam said zero-burning statements were not enough and that companies must produce evidence.
He said Singapore would use every legal and regulatory lever it has, including pressure on access to financing.
Banks had already put questions to the firms, he added, and the government would also review whether linked companies receive Singapore grants or incentives, and was prepared to amend laws urgently if needed.
For shareholders, the risk now goes beyond reputation to funding costs and capital access.
Public dollars draw private money into Singapore equities
EQDP has attracted more than S$1 of private capital for every dollar of public funds invested.
National Development Minister Chee Hong Tat, who is also deputy chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), gave the figure at the Securities Investors Association (Singapore) Investors’ Choice Awards on 21 October 2026.
The programme is now in its third phase.
After the third batch of fund managers was named in September, cumulative allocations reached S$5.4 billion across 14 asset managers.
Turnover among Next 50 constituents is up 93% from 2025, and more
small- and mid-cap stocks
can now absorb institutional flows.
More reforms are planned:
MAS and SGX RegCo aim to streamline listing reviews from January 2027.
IPO guides tailored to retail investors are being developed.
A public consultation on the revised Code of Corporate Governance is due next week.
Mr Chee also linked governance to the haze issue.
He warned that enforcement against errant firms could hurt their shareholders’ investments as well as the companies themselves.
Keppel REIT doubles down on CBD offices with sponsor deal
Keppel REIT
(SGX: K71U) announced on 20 October 2026 that it will buy a 51% stake in Keppel South Central from its sponsor,
Keppel Ltd
(SGX: BN4), for S$610.9 million.
The 33-storey Grade A building has 522,500 sq ft of net lettable area and is valued at about S$1.2 billion, or roughly S$2,350 per square foot (psf).
The deal raises Keppel REIT’s Singapore exposure to 82%.
It also offers pro forma distribution per unit accretion of 2.01% and an initial property yield of 4.3%.
As at 15 October 2026, about 60% of the space was under committed leases or leases being documented.
Keppel will provide guaranteed monthly income of S$2.23 million for up to five years.
Funding will come from a mix of bank loans, perpetual securities, internal cash and/or equity, taking aggregate leverage to 39.2%.
Jefferies kept its “hold” rating and S$0.85 target price.
It flagged a possible overhang from equity fundraising and questions about the asset’s underlying yield before stabilisation.
Unitholders will vote on the deal in the fourth quarter of 2026 (4Q2026), with completion expected in 2Q2027.
iFAST enters ETF issuance with four SGX listings
iFAST Corporation
(SGX: AIY) listed its first four exchange-traded funds (ETFs) on SGX on 22 October 2026, in partnership with DWS Group’s Xtrackers brand.
The suite comprises:
iFAST Xtrackers Artificial Intelligence & Big Data UCITS Index ETF (SGX: XBG)
iFAST Xtrackers Nikkei 225 UCITS Index ETF (SGX: JPY)
iFAST Xtrackers MSCI Korea UCITS Index ETF (SGX: KOR)
iFAST Xtrackers MSCI Taiwan UCITS Index ETF (SGX: TWD)
Each fund invests in an existing
Xtrackers UCITS ETF
.
Investors can trade the funds in Singapore dollars during local market hours, and eligible investors may use Supplementary Retirement Scheme (SRS) funds.
Depending on individual circumstances, the UCITS structure may also give Singapore investors different tax and estate-planning outcomes compared with holding overseas-listed securities directly.
Group CEO Lim Chung Chun called the listing “a new chapter for iFAST” as the group moves further up the investment value chain.
iFAST had S$36.13 billion in assets under administration as at 30 June 2026.
ETF issuance adds a potential new revenue stream, though its contribution will depend on how much in assets the funds gather.
Getty Images files for Chapter 11 to go private
Getty Images
(NYSE: GETY) said on 21 October 2026 that it had started voluntary Chapter 11 proceedings for some of its US subsidiaries in the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware.
The filing is part of a pre-packaged plan to restructure its debt.
Members of the Getty family and affiliates of Koch Equity Development will invest up to US$533 million (around S$681 million) to pay down debt.
Koch will also provide up to US$143 million in financing, which, together with cash from its ongoing operations, will let Getty operate normally during the process.
Getty expects to complete the restructuring by year-end, subject to regulatory approvals.
It will then become a private company owned by the equity investors.
The filing follows a difficult period.
Getty reported a loss of US$206.1 million in 2025 and was recently told its shares faced delisting from the New York Stock Exchange after falling below US$1.
The case shows how heavy debt can wipe out shareholder value when earnings weaken.

title: Swiss stocks becoming a haven from AI fears roiling markets
article:
(Oct 24): Shares of Switzerland’s ultra-defensive big companies are a bright spot in a tumultuous period for European equity markets.

The Swiss Market Index (SMI), which tracks the country’s 20 largest and most liquid stocks, has risen 4.6% this month while its euro-area counterpart, the Euro Stoxx 50, has fallen 3.2%. That outperformance of almost eight percentage points is the most by the Swiss benchmark since March 2020, when investors sought shelter from the shocks of the Covid-19 pandemic.

The gain shows how investors are paring back risk within Europe in the face of rising borrowing costs, scepticism around the artificial intelligence (AI) trade and political turmoil in countries like France and Spain.

The three biggest companies have driven the performance. Drugmakers Roche Holding AG and Novartis AG are up 12% and 6.7% respectively in October. The world’s largest food company, Nestlé SA, has rallied 10%. The three defensive stalwarts account for all of the benchmark’s advance this month.

Switzerland’s strength mirrors a broader pivot in Europe towards so-called defensives, whose fortunes don’t rise and fall as much with the cycles of the economy. Investors are favouring high-profitability companies with strong balance sheets that are less exposed to rising borrowing costs. The SMI is one of the biggest beneficiaries of that shift, given that Roche, Novartis and Nestlé account for almost half the index’s value.

See also: Stocks fall as oil rally keeps a lid on Treasuries

“Investors like the defensiveness of Swiss stocks and are actively looking for alternatives to the crowded AI trades,” said Damian Burkhardt, the head of Swiss equities at EFG Asset Management. “Healthcare was the funding sector for the AI trade and that is reversing now.”

Bank of America Corp’s latest fund manager survey also showed a sharp improvement in sentiment towards Swiss stocks, with a net 16% of respondents saying it’s their most preferred European equity market.

Shares of smaller index constituents also have gained, with fragrance maker Givaudan SA and dermatology company Galderma Group AG rising the most. Meanwhile, only four stocks in the SMI — all cyclical companies — are in the red this month.

See also: Watch out for the tall poppies

The change in fortunes follows a dry spell for the Swiss index, which is notorious for its limited exposure to this year’s winners in energy and technology. This decade, the SMI has returned 69% in local-currency terms including dividends, underperforming the Euro Stoxx 50, which has doubled.

The rally also reflects investor confidence over SMI companies’ accelerating earnings growth for 2027, which at 10% is set to be almost twice as strong as what is pencilled in for this year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence.

To be sure, a look at the SMI’s valuation raises questions how much further the rally has to go. The latest boon has pushed the benchmark back into what can be considered expensive territory when comparing to the past decade — both in absolute terms and relative to the Euro Stoxx 50, against which it is the most expensive in almost two years.

The earnings outlook for Switzerland’s export-dependent large-cap stocks has particularly been brightened by the weakening Swiss franc, which now trades versus the dollar at levels last seen in the first half of 2025. The currency also has weakened against the euro over the past seven months, though it’s recovered some of those losses this month as traders sought a hedge against political tensions in the euro area, particularly in France.

Swiss equity performance typically rests on interest rates, the dollar as well as a peaking macro cycle, according to Bank J Safra Sarasin equity strategist Wolf von Rotberg, who upgraded the country to outperform this month.

“All three factors have lately worked in the SMI’s favour,” von Rotberg said. “The roll-over at the beginning of the month came on the back of a peak in US macro momentum and provided the perfect backdrop for a recovery in beaten-up Swiss equities.”

title: Apple's iPhone Duo hits stores in face of short supply, high demand
article:
(Oct 24): Apple Inc quickly sold out of its limited in-store inventory for the new iPhone Duo, underscoring the strong demand for a foldable device that starts at nearly US$2,000 ($2,554).

The phone went on sale on Friday, bringing back the once-familiar sight of people lining up overnight to get their hands on it first. Marking the company’s most radical reinvention in the iPhone’s nearly two-decade history, the Duo is a major bet that Apple can establish itself in a category that’s remained a niche so far.

Apple’s latest gadget packed stores from New York to Beijing and Singapore. The early turnout featured customers collecting their pre-orders, some trying their luck to secure limited inventory for walk-in purchases, and resellers hoping to flip the devices for a higher price.

In Singapore, a few hundred people stood in line early on Friday, including a family of seven from Myanmar who had camped out overnight.

“This is the first true innovation Apple have had in years,” said Peter Ingram, a chief technology officer visiting from London, who plans to buy it upon his return to the UK. “It is expensive. But I tried it out, played with it in the store. It’s incredible how it’s got no crease.”

In the US, Apple stores received roughly 50 to 200-plus Duo units per location, and they went fast. A store in Los Angeles had no units left for people who arrived after around 6.30am. The 256-gigabyte star white model, priced at US$1,999, was popular with shoppers.

See also: UK said to push for carve-out from new EU tech sovereignty rules

Large crowds on launch day have mostly dissipated in recent years after Apple, retailers and wireless carriers began maintaining enough inventory to fulfill most orders through home delivery or appointment-based store pickups. But the company’s first foldable device arrived in much more limited supply.

Consumers placing new orders for the Duo on Apple’s website are now being offered delivery at the end of January, though some have seen their shipping estimates move up to as soon as November or December. The delays mark some of the lengthiest for a new Apple product in the company’s modern era.

Shoppers at the Domain Northside Apple Store in Austin were greeted by new chief executive officer John Ternus, who took the helm last month. At the Fifth Avenue location in New York, the line was already stretching multiple blocks around 5am, three hours before doors opened to iPhone Duo customers. The launch there was marked by Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice-president of marketing, and Vanessa Trigub, the vice-president of retail stores.

See also: AI video startup Higgsfield draws investment from Nvidia

At the Apple Store in Lawrence Township, New Jersey, about 40 miles outside Philadelphia, the 256- and 512-gigabyte configurations sold out within the first half hour, leaving the pricier one- and two-terabyte models.

Victor Osorio, a shopper at that location, said even though foldables aren’t new, “Apple always does something different and adds extra spice to it. I’m not nervous about the form factor but I am about the hinge. I don’t want it to get in the way but it looks OK so far.” Osorio arrived early with his partner, Victoria, who also purchased the Duo and said she was intrigued by the device’s multitasking capabilities.

At the same location, Naveed Abubacker said he trades in his iPhone every year. “Foldable technology has been around for a while and Apple is late to the gate but I’m ready for it,” he said. “If it doesn’t work out for me, I’ll return it.”

A display of iPhone Duo smartphones in London on Friday. Apple’s latest gadget has packed stores from New York to Beijing and Singapore.

In China, Shanghai and Beijing saw a moderate turnout, with most Duo buyers already loyal Apple customers who said they were excited to try out the new design. Many had to register in advance to secure their unit.

“It will take some getting used to,” said Andy Shen at Apple’s Sanlitun store in Beijing. “I chose the Duo mainly because it opens up to a bigger screen to enable better experience with videos, though its other functions are not measuring up to earlier generations, like the camera.”

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

As one of the most expensive mainstream smartphones ever sold, the Duo had raised questions about just how much demand there would be. Most of the shoppers in Beijing and Singapore looked past the high price and focused on the promise of a truly new Apple product after many years of iterative updates.

The iPhone line-up is Apple’s largest moneymaker, generating roughly half of the company’s revenue. And the Duo is the biggest single design change in the device’s nearly history. Though the company wasn’t first to market with a foldable phone, it looks to gain an edge with a more polished product built for Apple fans.

Rather than a repeat of the lacklustre debut of the Vision Pro headset nearly three years ago, the Duo’s launch is shaping up to be a throwback to the iPhone introductions of old — when demand far outstripped supply. That’s the case even with device prices reaching as high as US$3,199 for models with two terabytes of storage.

Though the Duo’s cost sets a record for a mass-market smartphone, Apple’s competitors such as Samsung Electronics Co, Xiaomi Corp and Oppo have been raising prices as well. Shortages of memory chips and other components have made consumer electronics more expensive across the board.

The new phones from Apple are difficult to produce because of their advanced hinge and new display technology. They are also only built in a limited number of facilities in China. Apple expanded production in recent years for its traditional iPhones, including to India, which has helped with supply.

Apple reports its quarterly earnings results on Nov 2, but those won’t include sales of the Duo because the period concluded around the end of September. It will reflect early sales of iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models, which debuted on Sept 18.

Other new versions, such as the entry-level iPhone or the updated Air, won’t go on sale until next year, Bloomberg News has reported. That marks a change in the company’s usual release schedule, a move meant to help spread out revenue across the year.

title: OpenAI resumes training AI — without internet access
article:
(Oct 24): OpenAI has begun cutting off internet access for its most capable artificial intelligence (AI) models during the training process in response to prior incidents in which its systems breached other companies.

The company said in a blog post on Friday that, after a pause last month, it had resumed training its most advanced models but intends to block internet access until it feels it has adequate safeguards in place to mitigate the risk of unreleased models being able to take unapproved actions online during training.

“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company wrote.

In late September, the company said it would pause training its most advanced AI models after it discovered that one of its AI agent systems that was being trained in what was supposed to be a secured, internet-free environment was able to gain access to the web to reach an external, third-party chatbot.

At the time, OpenAI described the breakout as the first security incident of its kind since a combination of models gained internet access during internal testing and inadvertently breached the system of the AI platform Hugging Face in July.

The models involved in the inadvertent Hugging Face breach were operating without the usual safety guardrails, the company has said, because OpenAI had intended them to remain in a testing area known as a “sandbox” — essentially, an isolated virtual software environment that’s meant to run security tests or analyse unsafe code in a controlled way. The models were able to break out of that sandbox, however, by leveraging a software vulnerability to access the open internet.

OpenAI said that after the Hugging Face incident, it reduced the connections through which its models might be able to reach the internet during training and testing but kept some for the purpose of metrics, logging and authentication. It also spent a vast amount of computing power on tasking agentic AI systems with identifying vulnerabilities in its training environments as part of a red-teaming effort, a phrase typically used to describe deliberate attempts to break into systems to uncover vulnerabilities before real attackers can.

“Our red-teaming agents found vulnerabilities in almost every one of these services that gave them limited forms of internet access,” the firm said in its post.

The company said it has since deployed software patches, imposed tighter network restrictions and disclosed the findings to vendors.

See also: Apple is Wall Street’s favourite AI haven as spending fears hit

There have been a series of disclosures in recent months from OpenAI and rivals including Anthropic PBC about incidents in which their models carried out self-directed attacks or unsanctioned actions on third-party websites and systems.

These cases, and a series of stark warnings from within the industry, have vaulted the safety debate into the mainstream. AI developers have warned that their systems could soon become too sophisticated for people to control, adding to concerns the technology could be used by malicious human actors to create bioweapons or carry out devastating cyberattacks.

title: Stocks fall as oil rally keeps a lid on Treasuries
article:
(Oct 24): A resurgence in oil prices dragged down stocks and bonds on Friday, stoking concerns about inflation just days ahead of the US Federal Reserve (Fed) decision on interest rates.

Brent crude settled near US$117 as a flare-up in Middle East violence threatened supplies. Most S&P 500 firms fell even as selling pressure on tech shares abated. A gauge of chipmakers edged up, but posted its longest weekly drop since November. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 1.2%. Treasuries relinquished a portion of the previous session’s rally.

Investors’ risk-off mood is likely to continue well into November, according to Bank of America Corp’s Michael Hartnett, a sign of how jitters around the artificial-intelligence (AI) trade and the midterm elections have held back US equities.

“We stay tactically risk-off until mid-November,” the strategist wrote in a note to clients on Friday. “Expect down-in-yields, down-in-stocks, down-in US dollar trade.”

The recent sell-off in AI-linked stocks is a reminder that the most popular trades tend to hurt the most when sentiment turns. When everyone owns the same story, even a small disappointment can set off a rush for the exits, according to Brian Jacobsen at Annex Wealth Management.

“The practical takeaway is not to abandon growth stocks, but to check whether one theme has quietly grown to dominate your portfolio after a long run,” he said. “Rebalancing, which means trimming what has grown too large and adding to what has lagged, is a simple way to keep risk in check without trying to predict the next move.”

See also: Watch out for the tall poppies

“Four forces explain this week’s yo-yo: a solid earnings season and attractive bond yields on one side, the cost of financing and more selective sovereign stress on the other,” said Florian Ielpo at Lombard Odier Asset Management.

The problem is not that equities are pricey, it’s that bonds are no longer expensive, he said.

“The latest moves do not alter our view that robust earnings should continue to support equities,” said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Chief Investment Office. “AI demand remains strong, current bond yields provide attractive income, and geopolitical developments alone do not justify a broadly defensive investment stance.”

See also: AI trade stumbles after tech earnings; oil gains

The Fed has been clear that it’s aware AI is boosting US demand. With inflation above target across a range of measures, leaning against that impulse through modest rate adjustments and tighter financial conditions is sensible policy, according to Tiffany Wilding at Pacific Investment Management Co.

“However, the economic adjustments now underway could evolve in several ways, and inflation is elevated but not accelerating,” she said. “This likely gives the Fed room to take a measured approach.”
• SpaceX aims to secure a minimum of 80,000 cell sites across the US, and it’s in talks with at least one major cellular infrastructure company to reach that goal, according to people familiar with the matter.
• Apple Inc quickly sold out of its limited in-store inventory for the new iPhone Duo, underscoring the strong demand for a foldable device that starts at nearly US$2,000 ($2,554).
• American Express Co is cutting 5% of its headcount globally as chief executive officer Steve Squeri seeks to keep a lid on the company’s rising costs.
• SLB, the world’s biggest oil field services provider, said it has seen a gradual recovery in its Middle East business despite disruptions from the Iran war.
• Bristol Myers Squibb Co has reported a death in its clinical trials of an experimental cell therapy for autoimmune diseases, potentially adding to safety concerns about a promising new class of treatments.

• The S&P 500 was down 0.5% as of 4pm New York time
• The Nasdaq 100 was little changed

• Apple Inc has already shown there’s a strong appetite for its US$2,000-and-up foldable iPhone Duo. Now it needs to meet that demand. The new device went on sale on Friday, bringing back the once-familiar sight of people lining up overnight to get their hands on it first.
• American Express Co is cutting 5% of its headcount globally as chief executive officer Steve Squeri seeks to keep a lid on the company’s rising costs.
• SLB, the world’s biggest oil field services provider, said it has seen a gradual recovery in its Middle East business despite disruptions from the Iran war.
• Newmont Corp, the world’s biggest gold producer, surpassed forecasts on stronger-than-expected prices for the yellow metal.

“Rising oil is taking the baton from credit concerns as the main threat to the equity rotation that has been keeping the S&P 500 afloat,” says Michael Ball, Macro Strategist, Markets Live at Bloomberg Strategists.

title: NYSE options exchange trading halted by ‘technical issue’
article:
(Oct 24): A NYSE options exchange has suspended trading, causing other exchanges to disregard quotes from the venue.

NYSE American Options has halted trading in some options securities, according to a notification from the exchange.

The exchange is one of 20 options venues, accounting for about 10% of the more than 70 million contracts of US equity options that trade each day.

Other exchanges are now ignoring any quotes from NYSE American Options, according to exchange statements. Options exchanges typically do not let orders execute at a worse price to one shown on another exchange. In the event of a system malfunction, such as this, that rule can be disregarded.
